turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mr Pillay, sit. Repeat scripts, pharmacy list is open, and we're already running late.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. Bench since before seven. I'm finished, hey, and this knee is the whole reason I came.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which knee?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The right one. And I want something stronger than Panado. The repeats can wait a minute.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has it been sore?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Right knee, for years. Since the cold set in it's worse, and at night I can't get comfortable.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Out of ten, right now.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Seven in this chair. Eight walking to the spaza.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Swelling?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. Looks a bit full at night, then it's flat by morning.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stiff in the morning?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, the right knee. About twenty minutes, till I walk around the kitchen. Then it eases.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Short of breath?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I'm not.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stomach burning at the moment?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Not now. I stopped the Voltaren in March. It was burning a hole in me.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Dose?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Fifty milligrams, twice a day, by mouth. Only for the knee. Not one since March.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pharmacy list says amlodipine five milligrams once daily, Panado one gram three times a day, and naproxen two hundred and fifty milligrams that was never collected.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine, ja, I've had high blood pressure for years. But I take ten milligrams, not five. One in the morning. Chemist gives me the tens.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): This list says five. You're certain it's ten?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Certain. Ten is on the tablet. Don't cut me to five or my pressure will climb.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the Panado, one gram three times a day — every dose?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): So which ones do you actually take?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Morning and bedtime, mostly. I miss the midday one. I was going to say when I'm at work — well, actually I'm retired. Took the package. Still forget lunch.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Naproxen. Did you ever take it?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Didn't collect it. Not even once.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Write tramadol then. My neighbour's on it, she says it's the only tablet that works.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): No tramadol.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, why? Panado is chalk. I hardly slept last night, I'm cross, and you just say no.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Opioid. Makes people drowsy. This is a script review, not a place to start that.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): The not sleeping was the knee and load shedding. Fan died, room was an oven. I know that's a tangent. I still want proper pain tablets.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pressure this morning was one hundred and forty-eight over ninety-two. Pulse seventy-six.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): High, then. I've been stressed, that's all.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alcohol?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): One beer some Saturdays. Not every week. That's it.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Medicine allergies?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any operations?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never been cut.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Diabetes medicine, or any other tablet at home?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): No diabetes. Just the blood pressure one and the Panado. Nothing else.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Family — joints or heart disease?
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother had knees like mine. Can't tell you about my father, he wasn't around.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Knee exam. No redness, not warm, no real effusion. You flex to about ninety degrees and stop. Medial joint line is tender.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm calling this wear and tear — osteoarthritis of the right knee, provisional. Not an infection, and tramadol won't fix the mechanics.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): So no Myprodol, no codeine, nothing stronger.

[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Correct, none of those. I'll renew the Panado, one gram morning and night, and a third dose only if you actually remember. Bring the amlodipine box next visit — I'm not changing five to ten blind.

[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): If walking is still this limited in six weeks, we'll book an x-ray of the right knee. Not today. Come back in three months for the script, sooner if the knee locks or you get chest pain.

spec.situation: Routine repeat-prescription review at a small clinic with a pharmacy technician present; patient wants a stronger painkiller; tablet names and doses are discussed in detail, one dose is read from the pharmacy list and differs from the patient's own; doctor declines the stronger medicine.
features: ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

bad.reason: Current stomach burning is denied; past burning from Voltaren is implied, not clearly stated as resolved symptom.
bad.text: Stomach burning (category=gastrointestinal, status=resolved, temporality=resolved, body_site=stomach, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: No tramadol/codeine/Myprodol supported; 'do not change amlodipine dose yourself' is not said to patient.
bad.text: Do not start tramadol, codeine, or Myprodol, and do not change the amlodipine dose yourself (action_type=counselling, status=recommended, responsible_person=patient)

omissions.text: Intermittent right knee swelling/fullness was reported: it sometimes looks a bit full at night and is flat by morning.
Naproxen 250 mg was on the pharmacy list but the patient said he never collected it and never took it even once.
Amlodipine dose is recorded incompletely/wrongly: the patient specifically said he takes 10 mg once each morning, not 5 mg, and warned not to reduce it because his blood pressure will climb.
